summary: Defines a set of reserved anycast addresses within each IPv6 subnet prefix, and lists their initial allocation. These addresses let a node reach a router or service on a subnet without knowing which specific one.

eli5.summary: Some addresses are set aside in every neighborhood to mean any one helper nearby. Whoever is closest and able answers the call.

subtitle: Sets aside the 128 highest interface identifier values in every IPv6 subnet as reserved anycast addresses.

tldr.problem: IPv6 anycast addresses let a packet reach the nearest of several nodes, but there was no agreed place inside a subnet to put well-known anycast addresses for specific services.
tldr.mechanism: The highest 128 interface identifier values in each subnet are reserved as anycast addresses, each picked by a 7-bit anycast ID, and they must never be used as unicast addresses.
tldr.outcome: The first allocation names anycast ID 126 (7E hex) for the Mobile IPv6 Home-Agents anycast address, with more IDs expected to follow.

today: RFC 2526 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the reserved subnet anycast address format and the initial allocation.

sections.title: Why Reserve Anycast Addresses
sections.content:
An anycast address is assigned to one or more network interfaces, typically on different nodes. A packet sent to it is delivered to the 'nearest' interface that has the address, as measured by the routing protocols in use.

The RFC gives two example uses: letting nodes reach one of a collection of servers for a well-known service without configuring a server list in each node, and forcing a source route through a specific internet service provider without naming one specific router. IPv6 already requires a Subnet-Router anycast address for all routers in a subnet prefix. This document adds a set of reserved anycast addresses inside each subnet prefix.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you want to call 'any helper' instead of one particular person. This document sets aside special addresses so everyone knows where to call.

sections.title: How the Addresses Are Built
sections.content:
Within each subnet, the highest 128 interface identifier values are reserved as subnet anycast addresses. The interface identifier holds a 7-bit anycast ID, and the remaining higher-order bits are all ones.

For address types that must use 64-bit interface identifiers in EUI-64 format, these are format prefixes 001 through 111, except multicast (1111 1111). The universal/local bit MUST be set to 0 (local) in these addresses, because the identifier is not globally unique. The layout is a 64-bit subnet prefix, then 57 bits of 1111110111...111, then the 7-bit anycast ID.

For other address types, the interface identifier may be other than 64 bits and is not in EUI-64 format. The layout is an n-bit subnet prefix, then 121-n bits of ones, then the 7-bit anycast ID.

The addresses come from the IPv6 unicast address space and are reserved on all links with all subnet prefixes. They MUST NOT be used as unicast addresses on any interface.
sections.eli5: The last 128 house numbers on every street are saved for helpers. Each one has a short code at the end that says which kind of helper it is.

sections.title: Why the Highest Values
sections.content:
The RFC reserves the highest addresses rather than the lowest to avoid clashing with existing official and unofficial uses of low-numbered addresses. Those are often used for the ends of a point-to-point link, for tunnel endpoints, for manually configured unicast addresses when no hardware token is available, and even for statically configured routers on a link.

Only 128 values are reserved, rather than perhaps 256. This means the minimum possible size of an interface identifier is 8 bits, which leaves room for unicast addresses as well, and lets the split between subnet prefix and interface identifier fall on a byte boundary.
sections.eli5: The low house numbers are already used by lots of people, so the helper numbers go at the far end of the street where nobody lives.

sections.title: The Allocated Anycast IDs
sections.content:
The RFC defines the initial list of anycast IDs. ID 126 (7E hex) is the Mobile IPv6 Home-Agents anycast address. ID 127 (7F) is reserved, and so are IDs 0 to 125 (00 to 7D).

Additional anycast IDs are expected to be defined in the future.
sections.eli5: Only one helper number has a job so far. The rest are kept free for later.

sections.title: Worked Example: Home-Agents
sections.content:
The RFC builds the Mobile IPv6 Home-Agents address, anycast ID 126 (7E hex), in two ways. For a 64-bit EUI-64 identifier, the subnet prefix is followed by the identifier 1111110111111111 1111111111111111 1111111111111111 1111111111111110, where the 7th bit is the universal/local bit and is 0.

For other address types, assuming a 64-bit identifier for comparison, the identifier is all ones except for the final 7-bit anycast ID, 1111110. The same general construction applies to identifiers of other lengths.
sections.eli5: To make the home-agent address, fill the end of the street number with ones, then write the helper's code in the last few spots.

sections.title: Assigning New Anycast IDs
sections.content: New anycast IDs MUST be reserved within all subnet prefixes, so assigning them requires centralized administration. New values SHOULD be assigned in descending numerical order, and are expected to be assigned only with IESG approval.
sections.eli5: Because a new helper number is used on every street, a central office hands them out, starting from the top.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Reserved anycast addresses create a security concern only by giving attackers a well-known address to attack. Placing a service at a specific reserved address lets an attacker focus on that service. The RFC says such attacks are best dealt with in each service that uses a reserved anycast address.

It also points to RFC 1546, which first proposed anycasting in IP, for security considerations of anycasting in general.
sections.eli5: A famous address is easy for bad guys to find too, so each service has to protect itself.
